strategy: Peer-to-peer conversational posts. No pitch, no case study numbers, no CTA in the post. Show up as a fellow business owner, ask questions that get real operators talking. Service the conversation in comments naturally.

scripts.content: Running a service business in 2026 is genuinely harder than it was 3 years ago. Not harder to do the work — harder to keep the pipeline full without bleeding money on ads. What's actually working for you guys right now to get consistent jobs?
Honest question for the business owners in here — if you could fix ONE thing about how your business runs right now, what would it be?
Most service businesses I talk to are either feast or famine. Never just steady. What broke that cycle for you — or are you still in it?
What's the part of running your business that you wish you could just hand off tomorrow?

The guys I see staying booked solid aren't necessarily the best at their craft. They just figured out the business side earlier. What was the thing that clicked for you when growth started feeling less random?
What was the hardest part of going from just you to your first hire? Not the paperwork. The mental part.

Nobody warns you how much of running a service business is just chasing people. Chasing leads. Chasing payments. Chasing reviews. What's the thing you spend the most time chasing that you wish ran itself?
At what point did referrals start coming in without you asking for them? Trying to understand what actually builds that kind of reputation vs. just hoping for it.
Do you charge what you're actually worth or what you think people will pay? Serious question. Most owners I talk to admit those two numbers are not the same.
How do you handle the slow months? Some guys I know use them to build systems. Others just grind through. Curious what actually works.
Paying for leads is a weird game. You pay more, get more volume, but quality gets worse. You pay less, you don't get enough. Anyone actually crack this, or is it always a trade-off?
When did getting reviews stop feeling awkward? Most guys either ask too hard or never ask at all. There's gotta be a middle ground that actually works.
What percentage of your jobs come from repeat customers vs. new ones? And do you do anything specific to keep people coming back or does it just happen?
What's the most expensive mistake you made in your first two years that you'd warn someone else about?
There seems to be a wall a lot of service businesses hit around the $300-500k mark where everything that worked to get there stops working. Anyone been through that? What actually got you unstuck?
How many times do you follow up with a lead before you let it go? Most guys I talk to say once or twice. Wondering if there's a better answer.
At some point you have to stop being the guy who does everything and start being the guy who runs the business. What made that switch actually happen for you?
Are you seeing more competition in your market than 2 years ago, or is it staying about the same? Feels like every niche is getting more crowded but curious if that's local to me.
What's one tool or app that actually made a real difference in how you run your business? Not the ones everyone recommends. The one that actually stuck.
Real question — if you had to start your business over from zero tomorrow, what would you do completely differently?

drafts_pending_approval.focus: ads pain — missed call / lead leakage
drafts_pending_approval.content: How much of your ad spend is going to calls you never answered? Not bad leads — I mean someone called, you were on a job, they moved on. Most service businesses have no idea what that number is because there's no record of what you didn't pick up. Anyone actually tracking that gap?

Anyone actually using AI in their business right now — not reading about it, actually using it day to day? Not looking for a pitch. Genuinely curious what's stuck around and what turned out to be a waste of time.

drafts_pending_approval.focus: ads pain — cost per booked job vs cost per lead
drafts_pending_approval.content: What's your actual cost per booked job right now? Not cost per lead. Most guys I talk to only track the first number — which means they don't really know if their ads are working or just generating activity.

drafts_pending_approval.focus: ads pain — lead follow-up / speed to response
drafts_pending_approval.content: How fast do you typically respond to a new inbound lead? Asking because most of the guys I talk to think they respond fast, but when you actually look at the timestamps it's hours — sometimes the next morning. Curious if that's just the reality of running a field service business.

Do you have any system for leads who ghost you after a quote, or do you just let them go cold? Most of the time those people are still shopping and just got distracted. Wondering if anyone's actually solved this or if it's still manual.
